Long-standing rumours suggest Apple is working on a foldable, clamshell-style device, possibly an iPad, a Mac, both, or some hybrid of the two.

Recent reports claim the project has been cancelled, despite it having been a priority for incoming CEO John Ternus — but I don't think that's entirely accurate…

Personally, I think the idea of a Mac/iPad hybrid is essentially obsolete. Macs can now run iPhone and iPad apps, and for many of us, iPhone Mirroring serves a similar purpose. We are also seeing increasing convergence between the two operating systems, and I believe this trend will continue: we are long past the days of Apple's old debate about merging a fridge and a toaster.

But I do believe that one day we will have an all-screen foldable Mac — provided the technology matures to the point where a soft keyboard can become a viable alternative to a hard one. This won't happen in the short term, but it will happen.

The dynamic keyboard transition phase

I think this is still a long way off, because I believe there will be an intermediate phase: the dynamic hardware keyboard. I argued a decade ago why I thought this was the future; although the technology exists today in some niche applications, it has yet to enter the mainstream.

One early example was the Sonder Keyboard, which used tiny e-ink displays to re-label and remap keys.

For instance, for someone who spends all day editing in Final Cut Pro, a QWERTY keyboard is largely useless — which is why both physical keyboards and keyboard covers exist.

Wouldn't it be smarter if our MacBook keyboards, or desktop Magic Keyboards, could automatically re-label themselves to match the app in use?

A soft keyboard that feels like a hard one

However, the longer-term goal is a fully soft keyboard. Back in 2016, I noted that the arguments Steve Jobs made for virtual keys when launching the iPhone apply equally to the Mac keyboard.

Of course, soft keyboards have three problems:

  • A glass keyboard is uncomfortable to type on
  • We rely on key travel for feedback and comfort
  • Touch typists need to be able to feel where the keys are before pressing them

Apple already holds patents addressing each of these. First, using a flexible display rather than conventional glass allows the surface to deform when a virtual key is pressed. The second can be addressed by combining that deformation with haptic motors. And for the third — the need to physically feel the keys — there are two approaches.

Apple's patent uses electrostatic charges to let users perceive changes in surface texture. In other words, the surface can remain flat, but applying a charge to the display surface creates the sensation of physical keys. In 2023, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University proposed an alternative.

It's a question of when, not whether

Of course, all of this is still at a very early stage, but we only need to look at the Mac trackpad. These trackpads still sound and feel like mechanical devices, yet for years they have been solid-state units using haptics to simulate a physical click — and the effect is remarkably convincing.

Soft keyboards will eventually reach the same level of refinement. Whether through Apple's current proposals or technologies not yet conceived, they will solve those three problems.

When that day comes, Steve's argument will apply equally to the Mac. In clamshell mode, the keyboard would assume whatever form best suits the task at hand. When all we want is one giant display — whether for watching a movie or drawing with an Apple Pencil — we simply unfold it to get double the screen area.

So I'm perfectly open to the idea that the first-generation device may have been put on hold for now, but that is absolutely not the same as saying it has been cancelled. The time for this technology will come.

Those are my thoughts — what are yours? Please share them in the comments.
